overview: This domain covers the daily work of keeping an organization's information safe, and what happens when something goes wrong. It starts with protecting data itself through classification, handling, masking, sanitization and encryption, then moves to watching systems through logs, triage and threat intelligence, responding to incidents, protecting assets through their lifecycle, and testing defenses. Throughout, the entry-level practitioner follows policy and procedure, protects people first, stays within their role and escalates to the right owner or the incident response team instead of acting alone.
analogy: Think of a hospital. Patient records are sorted by sensitivity and handled by strict rules (data security). Monitors at every bed feed a central station, where staff decide which alarm needs attention first (security operations). When a patient's condition crashes, a trained team runs a rehearsed procedure in which everyone has a role (incident response). Equipment is tracked, maintained and retired safely (asset protection), and drills and inspections check that it all works (security testing). A new nurse who hears an alarm does not operate alone: they call the response team.

topics.overview: Data is protected by first deciding how sensitive it is, then handling it by rules that match that level until it is safely destroyed. This topic covers classification and labeling, handling and retention, masking and tokenization, media sanitization, the cryptography that protects data, and keeping sensitive data out of public AI services.
can_do: Tell classification from labeling, and name who sets a data set's classification
Pick clear, purge or destroy for a device, and explain why deleting files is not sanitization
Match symmetric encryption, asymmetric encryption, hashing and digital signatures to the job each does
Explain why pasting sensitive data into a public AI service is a disclosure

subtopics.name: Data Classification and Labeling
subtopics.definition: Data classification sorts information into sensitivity levels, such as public, internal, confidential and restricted, so each level gets protection that fits its value and risk.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without classification, everything gets the same protection: too little for secrets, too much for public brochures. Labels make the level visible, so people and tools know which handling rules apply.
how_it_works: Classification is decided by the business manager accountable for the data, called the data owner.
Levels reflect the harm caused if the data were disclosed, altered or lost, so the most damaging data gets the highest level.
A label then marks the level where people and systems can see it: a header, footer, watermark, file tag or metadata field.
Tools such as data loss prevention (DLP) read labels to warn or block when restricted data heads somewhere unsafe.
Owners review levels over time, because sensitivity changes, for example once a product launches.

rows.label: Who does it
cells: Users and systems apply the mark the owner set

rows.label: Output
cells: A visible or machine-readable mark on the data

rows.label: If it is missing
cells: No one knows what protection is needed
People guess, and tools cannot enforce the rules

subtopics.example: At a city council, a planning officer saves a report on land the council plans to buy, with no label, in a team-wide folder. Priya, a new security analyst, notices it. Rather than relabeling it themselves, Priya asks the report's owner, the planning director, to set its level, then helps apply the matching label and folder permissions the director chooses.

review: Apply the label your policy requires when you create or receive data
Use the label to choose where data may be stored and shared
evidence: The data classification policy and its defined levels
Labels and access settings on shared folders and files
audit_focus.recommend: Report mislabeled or unlabeled sensitive data to its owner, or to your supervisor if the owner is unknown.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner sets and changes the classification level

subtopics.isaca_rule: The owner decides the level; everyone else applies and respects it. When data is unlabeled or looks mislabeled, ask the owner rather than guessing, and protect it at the higher level until they answer.

exam_traps.trap: The IT team or a security analyst should decide how sensitive a business file is.
exam_traps.why: IT and security staff protect data but do not own it. The accountable business owner understands the harm of disclosure, so the owner sets the level.

exam_traps.trap: Labeling a file is the same as classifying it.
exam_traps.why: Classification is the decision about sensitivity; the label only records that decision. A label applied without the owner's decision may be wrong.

key_terms.definition: The person accountable for a data set, who sets its classification and approves who may access it.
The person or team that looks after data day to day, such as backups, following the owner's rules.
Tools that spot sensitive data by label or content and warn, block or log when it is moved unsafely.

subtopics.memory_aid: Owner decides, label shows, controls follow.

subtopics.name: Data Handling Across the Lifecycle
subtopics.definition: Data handling is the set of rules for how each classification level is created, stored, used, shared, archived and destroyed, from the moment data exists until it is gone.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Data often leaks while being used or shared, not while stored. Rules for every stage, including retention and destruction, close those gaps and keep the organization within the law.
how_it_works: The lifecycle runs create, store, use, share, archive and destroy, and each stage has rules for the data's level.
Handling rules cover where data may be stored, who may see it, how it is sent, and whether it may be printed or copied.
A retention schedule says how long each type of record is kept, based on legal, regulatory and business needs.
When retention ends, data is destroyed by a method that fits its level.
A legal hold, issued by legal counsel, pauses destruction of records that may be needed for a lawsuit or investigation.
subtopics.example: A logistics firm's policy says confidential customer records may be emailed only inside the company and must be encrypted on removable media. A sales manager asks Jordan, a help desk technician, to copy a customer list onto an unencrypted USB drive for a trade show. Jordan explains the handling rule, offers an approved encrypted drive instead, and logs the request as the procedure requires.

review: Follow the handling rule for the data's label before sharing or copying it
Use only approved storage and transfer methods for sensitive data
evidence: The handling matrix listing rules for each classification level
Legal hold notices listing which records must be preserved
audit_focus.recommend: Raise any request to bypass a handling rule with your supervisor, and send legal hold questions to legal counsel.
audit_focus.decides: Management sets handling rules in policy; legal counsel issues and lifts legal holds

subtopics.isaca_rule: Handling rules follow the label at every stage, including after data leaves your system. Keep data only as long as the retention schedule says, and never destroy records under a legal hold, even if their retention period has ended.

exam_traps.trap: Keeping all data forever is the safest choice.
exam_traps.why: Data kept past its retention period can still leak and can still be demanded in a lawsuit. Keeping it longer than needed adds risk and can break privacy law.

exam_traps.trap: Once retention ends, records under a legal hold can be deleted on schedule.
exam_traps.why: A legal hold overrides the schedule. Destroying held records can be treated as destroying evidence, so destruction waits until legal counsel lifts the hold.

key_terms.definition: The stages data passes through: create, store, use, share, archive and destroy.
A list of record types and how long each must be kept before it is destroyed.
An instruction from legal counsel to preserve specific records, suspending their normal destruction.

subtopics.name: Data Masking and Tokenization
subtopics.definition: Data masking hides real values behind realistic fakes or partial views, and tokenization swaps a sensitive value for a random token that maps back only through a secure vault.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Many people and systems need to work with data without seeing the real sensitive values. Masking and tokenization let testing, support and analytics go ahead while shrinking how much real data is exposed.
how_it_works: Static masking makes a changed copy, such as a test database with fake names, so real values never reach the test team.
Dynamic masking changes only what a viewer sees, such as the last four card digits, while the stored record stays intact.
Tokenization keeps the real value in a protected token vault and gives other systems a token with no mathematical link to it.
Only authorized systems can swap a token back for the real value, so fewer systems hold sensitive data.
Anonymized data can no longer identify anyone; pseudonymized data can be re-linked, so it still counts as personal data.

rows.label: Where the real value is
cells: Not in the masked copy at all

rows.label: Reversible?
cells: The view only; data is unchanged

rows.label: Typical use
cells: Payment card numbers and account IDs

subtopics.example: A school's software team needs realistic student records to test a new grade portal, and a developer suggests copying the live database to the test server. Sam, the junior security analyst on the project, points to the policy that bans live personal data in test systems and asks the database administrator for a statically masked copy, with fake names and birth dates.

review: Request masked or synthetic data for testing, never a live production copy
Use tokens or masked views in reports when full values are not needed
evidence: Test environments for real personal or payment data
Who can reach the token vault and turn tokens back into values
audit_focus.recommend: Report real sensitive data found in a test or support system to its data owner and your supervisor.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner approves any use of real data outside production

subtopics.isaca_rule: Give each person and system the least real data the task needs. Use masked data for testing and support, tokens where systems only need a reference, and keep the real values in as few places as possible.

exam_traps.trap: Tokenization is just another name for encryption.
exam_traps.why: Anyone with the key can decrypt an encrypted value. A token has no mathematical link to the original; only the vault can map it back.

exam_traps.trap: Masking a customer's name on screen means the database no longer holds it.
exam_traps.why: Dynamic masking changes only what the viewer sees. The real value is still stored and still needs full protection.

key_terms.definition: The tightly protected store that holds real values and their matching tokens.
Removing or changing identifiers so individuals can no longer be identified, even by combining data sets.
Replacing identifiers with substitutes while keeping a separate way to re-link them; the data is still personal data.

subtopics.name: Media Sanitization: Clear, Purge and Destroy
subtopics.definition: Media sanitization makes data on storage media infeasible to recover before the media is reused, leaves the organization's control or is discarded, using the clear, purge or destroy method.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Deleting files or formatting a drive removes the pointers, not the data, so free tools can bring it back. Retired laptops, copiers and phones have leaked records this way.
how_it_works: The method depends on the data's sensitivity, the media type, and whether the media will be reused or leave the organization.
Overwriting tools built for magnetic hard drives miss spare cells on solid-state drives (SSDs), so flash media needs a purge command or cryptographic erase.
For cloud storage, where the customer cannot reach the physical disks, cryptographic erase may be the only purge option.
Degaussing works only on magnetic media, and drilling a hole can leave readable areas, so neither is a dependable shortcut.
Each sanitization is verified and recorded, often on a certificate of sanitization, before the asset record is closed.

rows.label: Stops
cells: Simple recovery through the device's normal interface

rows.label: Typical technique
cells: Built-in sanitize command or cryptographic erase
Disintegrate, incinerate or melt; shred paper

rows.label: Good fit
cells: Reuse inside the organization for lower-sensitivity data
Reuse or resale, including outside the organization
Failed or obsolete media, and all paper

subtopics.example: A hospital is returning 40 leased laptops with solid-state drives. A facilities supervisor asks Alex, an IT support technician, to 'just format them' to save time. Alex explains that formatting would leave patient data recoverable, runs the approved purge tool on each drive, records each serial number and result, and sends the sanitization records to the asset manager.

review: Use the approved sanitization tool and method listed for the media type
Verify each device and record its serial number and method
evidence: Certificates of sanitization from any disposal or recycling vendor
Asset inventory entries updated as each device is released
audit_focus.recommend: Stop and tell your team lead when a device cannot be sanitized as the procedure requires, such as a failed drive.
audit_focus.decides: Policy and the data owner set the required method for each level

subtopics.isaca_rule: Deleting is not sanitizing. Match the method to the data and the media's destination: clear for low-risk internal reuse, purge before sensitive media leaves your control, destroy when it cannot be purged or reused. Verify and keep the record.

exam_traps.trap: Deleting the files and emptying the recycle bin sanitizes a laptop.
exam_traps.why: Deletion removes only the file pointers. The data stays on the drive until it is overwritten, and free tools can recover it.

exam_traps.trap: Degaussing is the right way to sanitize a solid-state drive.
exam_traps.why: Degaussing uses magnetic force and does nothing to flash storage. SSDs need a purge technique, such as cryptographic erase, or destruction.

key_terms.definition: A purge technique that destroys the keys protecting encrypted data, leaving only unreadable ciphertext.
A record of which media was sanitized, by what method, by whom, when, and how it was verified.
Media sanitization guidelines from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), published September 2025.

subtopics.name: Symmetric and Asymmetric Encryption
subtopics.definition: Encryption turns readable plaintext into unreadable ciphertext with an algorithm and a key; symmetric encryption uses one shared key, while asymmetric encryption uses a public and private key pair.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Encryption keeps data confidential even when it is stolen or intercepted. Choosing the wrong type, or losing control of keys, can leave data exposed or make it unrecoverable.
how_it_works: Symmetric algorithms such as the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) are fast, so they protect bulk data such as disks, databases and network sessions.
In asymmetric encryption, such as RSA (named after its inventors) or elliptic curve cryptography (ECC), anyone may use the public key, but only the owner holds the private key.
To send someone a secret, encrypt it with their public key; only their private key can decrypt it.
Real systems are hybrid: Transport Layer Security (TLS) uses asymmetric methods to agree on a session key, then symmetric encryption for the data.

rows.label: Keys
cells: A public key and a matching private key

rows.label: Speed
cells: Fast; suits large volumes of data
Slower; suits small items such as keys and signatures

rows.label: Main challenge
cells: Sharing the key safely with each party
Proving a public key really belongs to its owner

rows.label: Typical uses
cells: Key exchange, digital signatures and certificates

subtopics.example: An accounting firm partner encrypts a client's tax spreadsheet and plans to email it with the password typed in the same message. Morgan, the firm's IT assistant, explains that anyone intercepting the email would get both the locked file and its key. Morgan suggests the secure client portal instead, or at least sharing the password by phone, as the firm's policy requires.

review: Use approved encryption tools rather than inventing your own scheme
Send passwords or keys through a different channel from the data
evidence: Devices and data stores missing required encryption at rest
Certificate and key expiry dates in the key management service
audit_focus.recommend: Report a lost, exposed or shared private key to the key's owner and the security team immediately.
audit_focus.decides: Security management approves algorithms, key lengths and key handling rules

subtopics.isaca_rule: Use symmetric encryption for speed and bulk data, and asymmetric for exchanging keys and proving identity. Encrypt to someone with their public key. Encryption is only as strong as its key protection, so keep keys apart from the data.

exam_traps.trap: To send a confidential message, encrypt it with your own private key.
exam_traps.why: Anything encrypted with your private key opens with your public key, which anyone can have. For confidentiality, use the recipient's public key.

exam_traps.trap: Asymmetric encryption is stronger, so use it for all bulk data.
exam_traps.why: Asymmetric encryption is much slower and is not designed for large volumes. Systems use it to exchange a symmetric key, then encrypt the data symmetrically.

key_terms.definition: Creating, storing, rotating, backing up and destroying keys under control; strong encryption fails if keys are exposed.
A tamper-resistant device that creates and stores keys and uses them without ever exposing them.
Data at rest (stored), in transit (moving over a network) and in use (being processed); each needs protection.

subtopics.memory_aid: One shared key: symmetric. A public and private pair: asymmetric.

subtopics.name: Hashing and Digital Signatures
subtopics.definition: A hash function turns any input into a fixed-length digest that cannot be reversed; a digital signature applies the signer's private key to a hash to prove origin and integrity.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Hashing shows whether data has changed, and it protects stored passwords. Signatures add proof of who sent the data, so a sender cannot credibly deny it later.
how_it_works: Changing even one character of the input produces a completely different digest, so matching digests show the data is unchanged.
Hashing uses no key and cannot be undone, which is why it gives integrity, not confidentiality.
Passwords are stored as salted hashes made with deliberately slow algorithms, so a stolen password file is hard to crack.
To sign, software hashes the message and applies the sender's private key; anyone can verify the signature with the sender's public key.
Older algorithms such as Message Digest 5 (MD5) and Secure Hash Algorithm 1 (SHA-1) are broken for collisions; use current ones such as SHA-256 or SHA-3.

rows.label: Reversible?
cells: Checked with the public key, not reversed

rows.label: Example use
cells: Protecting a file or a session

subtopics.example: A university's IT team receives an email, apparently from a vendor, with an urgent firmware update for its campus parking meters. Before installing it, Casey, a junior systems administrator, checks the file's signature with the vendor's published public key and compares its hash with the vendor's website. The signature fails, so Casey does not install it and reports the email to the security team.

review: Install only software and updates whose signature verifies
Store passwords only with the approved hashing method, never as plain text
evidence: Signature verification results on updates and scripts
Systems still using MD5 or SHA-1 for integrity or signatures
audit_focus.recommend: Report any signature that fails to verify, or a hash that does not match, to the security team before going further.
audit_focus.decides: Security management decides which algorithms are approved

subtopics.isaca_rule: A hash proves nothing changed; it hides nothing and uses no key. A signature proves who sent something and that it is unchanged, but it does not keep it secret. When data must also be confidential, encrypt it as well.

exam_traps.trap: Hashing a customer file keeps it confidential.
exam_traps.why: A hash is not encryption. Hashing leaves the original file readable, and a hash cannot be decrypted back. Confidentiality needs encryption.

exam_traps.trap: A digitally signed email is also encrypted.
exam_traps.why: A signature proves origin and integrity, but anyone can still read the message. Confidentiality needs separate encryption with the recipient's public key.

key_terms.definition: A random value added to each password before hashing, so identical passwords produce different hashes.
Two different inputs that produce the same digest; once collisions can be made on purpose, the algorithm is broken.
Proof that a specific party sent or approved something, so they cannot credibly deny it.

subtopics.name: Quantum-Resistant Cryptography
subtopics.definition: Quantum-resistant, or post-quantum, cryptography uses public-key algorithms designed to stay secure even against a future quantum computer that could break today's RSA and elliptic curve methods.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Attackers can record encrypted traffic now and decrypt it once a capable quantum computer exists. Data that must stay secret for years is already at risk, and replacing algorithms across an organization takes years.
how_it_works: A large enough quantum computer could solve the math behind RSA and elliptic curve cryptography, breaking today's key exchange and digital signatures.
Symmetric encryption such as the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) and modern hash functions are far less affected; longer keys, such as AES-256, keep them strong.
In August 2024, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) published its first post-quantum Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS): 203, 204 and 205.
Migration starts with a cryptographic inventory: where each algorithm is used, what data it protects, and how long that data must stay secret.

types.meaning: A lattice-based method for two parties to agree on a shared key, replacing RSA or elliptic curve key exchange.
A lattice-based digital signature algorithm, intended as the main general-purpose replacement for today's signatures.
A hash-based digital signature algorithm, a backup built on different math in case lattice methods weaken.

subtopics.example: A health insurer keeps member records that must stay confidential for decades, and shares them with partners over links using RSA-based key exchange. The security manager asks Riley, a new analyst, to help start planning for quantum risk. Riley begins by listing each system, the algorithms it uses and how long its data must stay secret, so the manager can rank systems for migration.

review: Record algorithms and key lengths whenever you document a system
Flag systems protecting long-lived data that rely on RSA or elliptic curves
evidence: The migration priority list and the owner's sign-off on it
Vendor roadmaps for post-quantum support in key products
audit_focus.recommend: Raise systems that cannot change algorithms, such as embedded devices, with the system owner and security manager.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management sets migration priorities and funding

subtopics.isaca_rule: Quantum risk is a planning problem today. Start with an inventory, put long-lived secrets first, and favor crypto agility. Public-key algorithms need replacing; symmetric encryption mainly needs adequate key lengths.

exam_traps.trap: Quantum computers will break all encryption, so AES must be replaced too.
exam_traps.why: The main threat is to public-key algorithms such as RSA and elliptic curves. AES with long keys and modern hash functions are expected to stay secure.

exam_traps.trap: There is no risk until a quantum computer actually exists.
exam_traps.why: Encrypted data recorded today can be decrypted later. Data that must stay secret for years is already exposed to this harvest now, decrypt later threat.

key_terms.definition: Collecting encrypted data today in the hope of decrypting it once quantum computing makes that possible.
The ability to replace cryptographic algorithms in a system without a major redesign.
A list of where and how cryptography is used, including algorithms, key lengths and the data protected.

subtopics.memory_aid: Public-key is at risk, symmetric holds: list it, rank it, swap it.

subtopics.name: Data Leakage into Public AI Services
subtopics.definition: Data leakage into public artificial intelligence (AI) services happens when people paste or upload sensitive information into an AI tool their organization does not control.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A prompt is a data transfer. Depending on the service's terms, what users type may be stored, reviewed by the provider or used to train models, so confidential data, code or personal data can escape the organization's control.
how_it_works: Typing data into a public AI chatbot sends it to a third party, just like emailing it to an outside company.
An AI acceptable use policy says which tools are approved and which classification levels may be used with each.
Approved enterprise AI tools come with contracts covering data retention, training use and location, which free public tools usually lack.
Data loss prevention (DLP) and web filtering can warn or block when labeled data is pasted into unapproved AI sites.
Unapproved AI use is found through monitoring and the AI asset inventory, then brought under policy.
subtopics.example: Taylor, a customer service agent at a utility company, pastes a customer's account and payment history into a free public chatbot to help draft a reply, then remembers the company's AI policy. Instead of deleting the chat and saying nothing, Taylor reports it to the team lead and the security team, so they can assess the exposure under the incident procedure.

review: Check the AI policy and approved tools list before using AI for work
Remove sensitive details before using even an approved tool, where policy requires
evidence: The approved AI tools list, with each tool's data limits
DLP alerts for sensitive data sent to AI websites
audit_focus.recommend: Report sensitive data shared with an unapproved AI service to your supervisor and the security team at once.
audit_focus.decides: Management approves AI tools; the data owner decides what data may be used

subtopics.isaca_rule: Treat any public AI prompt as sharing data with an outsider. Use only approved AI tools, at the classification levels they are approved for, and report accidental sharing as a possible incident instead of hiding it.

exam_traps.trap: Deleting the chat history removes the data from the AI provider.
exam_traps.why: Deleting a conversation on screen may not remove copies the provider has already stored or logged. The exposure still needs to be reported and assessed.

exam_traps.trap: Public AI tools are fine for confidential work once the customer's name is removed.
exam_traps.why: Other details, such as account numbers, addresses or source code, can still identify people or reveal secrets. Follow the AI policy on what may be shared, and where.

key_terms.definition: AI tools or services used for work without the organization's approval or oversight.
Rules for how staff may use organization systems and services, including which AI tools are allowed.

topics.overview: Security operations is the daily watch over systems: collecting logs, spotting what matters among millions of events, and deciding what to do about it. This topic also covers who attacks and why, how threat intelligence and frameworks such as MITRE ATT&CK help defenders, and how AI can help or hurt alert triage.
can_do: Tell an event from an alert and an incident, and say when to escalate
Explain what to log, how to protect logs, and what a security information and event management (SIEM) system adds
Rank alerts by severity, asset value and confidence, and explain how correlation and AI cut noise
Match threat actors to likely motives, and describe how threat intelligence and ATT&CK are used

subtopics.name: Events, Alerts and Incidents
subtopics.definition: An event is anything observable on a system or network; an alert flags an event for review; an incident actually or imminently harms security or violates policy.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Treating every event as an incident wastes the response team's time, while treating a real incident as routine lets damage spread. Getting this call right decides when the incident response plan starts.
how_it_works: Systems produce huge numbers of events every day, and nearly all of them are normal business activity.
Monitoring rules turn a small share of events into alerts; an analyst checks each one and closes false alarms with a note.
The incident response plan defines what counts as an incident, often with examples, so the call is not left to personal judgment.
Declaring an incident starts the plan: the incident response team takes ownership, and severity decides who must be told.
Only authorized roles, such as the incident lead with legal counsel, decide whether an incident is a reportable breach.

types.meaning: Anything observable, such as a login, a file change or a blocked connection.
An event that a rule or tool flags as worth a person's review.
An occurrence that actually or imminently harms confidentiality, integrity or availability, or violates policy.
An incident in which data is confirmed to have been exposed to an unauthorized party.

subtopics.example: Overnight, a school district's monitoring tool alerts that a staff account logged in from two countries within an hour. Jamie, the analyst on shift, checks and finds the account then downloaded the payroll file. Because the plan lists unauthorized access to payroll data as an incident, Jamie stops investigating alone and escalates it, with notes, to the on-call incident response lead.

review: Compare what you see with the plan's incident definitions and examples
Write down what you checked before closing or escalating an alert
evidence: The alert's source, time, affected asset and account
Related events on the same host or account
audit_focus.recommend: Call the on-call incident lead as soon as an event looks like an incident, or whenever you are unsure.
audit_focus.decides: The incident lead declares incidents; legal counsel and management decide on notification

subtopics.isaca_rule: Not every event is an incident. Use the plan's definitions to decide, write down your reasoning, and once an event meets the incident threshold, hand it to the incident response team instead of carrying on alone.

exam_traps.trap: Every failed login or blocked connection should be reported as an incident.
exam_traps.why: These are normal events. Reporting them all floods the response team and hides real incidents. The plan's thresholds decide what is escalated.

exam_traps.trap: The analyst who finds exposed data should declare a breach and notify customers.
exam_traps.why: Breach notification is a legal decision with deadlines and wording rules. Escalate the facts; authorized roles, such as legal counsel and management, decide on notification.

key_terms.definition: An event with a negative effect, such as a system crash or a flood of failed logins; it may become an incident.
The formal point at which an event is treated as an incident and the response plan starts.

subtopics.name: Logging and Monitoring
subtopics.definition: Logging records who did what, when, where and with what result on systems and networks; monitoring reviews those records, often in a central tool, to spot problems quickly.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without logs, attacks go unseen and investigations have no evidence. Logs that nobody reviews, or that attackers can erase, give a false sense of safety.
how_it_works: Useful log entries record the user or process, the action, the time, the source and destination, and success or failure.
Every system syncs its clock to a trusted time source, so events from different logs line up in the right order.
Logs are sent to a central store that ordinary administrators cannot change, so an intruder cannot cover their tracks.
A security information and event management (SIEM) system collects logs, puts them in a common format and applies rules to raise alerts.
Logs are kept for a set retention period and can contain personal data, so they are protected like other sensitive records.
subtopics.example: At a regional bank, a server administrator notices that a file server's security log was cleared overnight. Because the server also sends its logs to the SIEM, Dana, a junior security operations center (SOC) analyst, can still see the earlier entries, which show a new administrator account created just before the clearing. Dana opens a ticket with these findings and escalates it to the incident response lead.

review: Confirm each new system sends logs to the SIEM before it goes live
Investigate when a log source suddenly stops sending
evidence: Log source coverage list showing which systems feed the SIEM
Time sync status across servers and network devices
audit_focus.recommend: Report cleared, altered or suddenly silent logs to the SOC lead as a possible sign of compromise.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides what is logged and how long logs are kept

subtopics.isaca_rule: Log what matters, sync every clock, and send logs somewhere the people being logged cannot alter. A cleared or silent log is itself a warning sign worth reporting, not a gap to ignore.

exam_traps.trap: Turning on logging is enough; review can wait until something goes wrong.
exam_traps.why: Unreviewed logs detect nothing. Monitoring, through rules, alerts and regular review, is what turns records into early warning.

exam_traps.trap: Keeping logs only on the server that creates them is fine if the server is secure.
exam_traps.why: An attacker who gains administrator rights can wipe local logs. A central, protected copy keeps the evidence.

key_terms.definition: Setting every system's clock from a common trusted source, often with the Network Time Protocol (NTP).
Assurance that log records have not been altered or deleted, for example through write-once or restricted storage.
Software on laptops and servers that records activity, detects threats and lets responders isolate the device.

subtopics.name: Event Triage: Use Cases, Prioritization and Correlation
subtopics.definition: Event triage is sorting incoming alerts to decide which are real, how urgent each is and who must act, using defined use cases, priority rules and correlation.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A security operations center (SOC) can receive thousands of alerts a day. Triage puts the dangerous few in front of analysts first, so a real attack is not lost among routine noise.
how_it_works: A use case defines one thing to detect, such as many failed logins followed by a success, with its data sources, rule and response steps.
Priority weighs the alert's severity, the value of the affected asset, and confidence that it is real: a payroll server outranks a test laptop.
Correlation links related events from different sources, such as a phishing email, a malware alert and an odd login, into one higher-priority case.
Routine events a tool already blocked, such as quarantined known malware, are logged; events needing a human decision are escalated.
Analysts close false positives with a reason and send recurring ones for rule tuning, rather than ignoring them.
Automation can add context, such as the asset owner and user history, before an analyst looks.

rows.label: What happens
cells: An alert fires on normal activity
A real attack raises no alert

rows.label: Cost
cells: Wasted analyst time and alert fatigue

rows.label: Usual fix
cells: Tune the rule so it fires less on normal activity
Add or improve the use case and its data sources

subtopics.example: At a parcel delivery company, the monitoring console shows three alerts: a printer offline, a blocked port scan from the internet, and a domain administrator account logging in at 3 a.m. from a warehouse kiosk it has never used. Lee, the analyst on duty, ranks the administrator login first, because it involves the most powerful account and matches a known use case, and follows its playbook.

review: Rank open alerts with the priority matrix before starting work
Correlate each alert with recent events for the same user and host
evidence: Asset criticality and owner for the affected system
Recent related alerts across email, endpoint and login logs
audit_focus.recommend: Escalate high-priority or correlated alerts to the incident response team as the playbook directs.
audit_focus.decides: The SOC lead approves rule tuning and changes to priority rules

subtopics.isaca_rule: Triage by impact, not by order of arrival. Rank alerts by severity, asset value and confidence, look for related events, and follow the playbook. Close nothing without a reason, and send noisy rules for tuning.

exam_traps.trap: Handle alerts strictly in the order they arrive, so nothing is skipped.
exam_traps.why: First in, first out can leave a critical alert waiting behind dozens of trivial ones. Priority rules put the riskiest first.

exam_traps.trap: A rule that produces many false positives should be switched off.
exam_traps.why: Disabling it may create false negatives for a real attack. Tune the rule through the proper change process instead.

key_terms.definition: Linking related events across sources and time to reveal an attack that single events would not show.
Step-by-step instructions for handling a specific type of alert or incident.

subtopics.name: AI-Driven Correlation and Alert Fatigue
subtopics.definition: Artificial intelligence (AI) correlation uses machine learning to group, rank and summarize security alerts; alert fatigue is when too many alerts cause analysts to miss real ones.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Overloaded analysts skim and close alerts on instinct, which is how real attacks slip past. AI can cut the noise, but trusted blindly or manipulated, it can hide the alerts that matter.
how_it_works: Machine learning in a security information and event management (SIEM) system groups related alerts into one case and removes duplicates.
It ranks cases by learned risk and can draft summaries, giving analysts a shorter, better-ordered queue.
Models can be wrong: aggressive suppression creates false negatives, and generated summaries can state facts the logs do not support.
Humans stay accountable: analysts check the evidence behind AI rankings, and changes to suppression rules go through approval.
Teams judge the tool by results, such as missed detections in tests and time to respond, not by how far alert counts fall.
subtopics.example: An airline's new AI-assisted SIEM cuts the daily queue from 4,000 alerts to 300 cases. A month later, Avery, a security analyst, finds the AI has been auto-closing alerts from one baggage-handling server as normal, including logins from an unknown account. Avery does not change the model's settings personally; they escalate the case and the suppression pattern to the security operations lead.

review: Open the raw events behind any AI-ranked case before closing it
Record cases where the AI ranking or summary was wrong
evidence: Alerts the AI suppressed or auto-closed during your shift
Detection test results showing whether known attacks still raise alerts
audit_focus.recommend: Report suspected AI misses, signs of poisoning or unexplained suppression to the security operations lead.
audit_focus.decides: The security operations lead approves AI tuning and suppression changes

subtopics.isaca_rule: AI should shrink the queue, not replace judgment. Check the evidence behind an AI ranking, treat its summaries as leads, and report suspected misses or odd suppression instead of quietly overriding the tool.

exam_traps.trap: Once AI correlation is in place, analysts can trust its priority ranking without checking.
exam_traps.why: AI rankings can be wrong or manipulated. Analysts confirm the underlying evidence, especially before closing a case as harmless.

exam_traps.trap: The cure for alert fatigue is to turn off most alert rules.
exam_traps.why: That trades noise for blindness. Reduce fatigue by tuning rules, correlating related alerts and automating enrichment, while testing that real attacks still raise alerts.

key_terms.definition: Automatically hiding or closing alerts judged low value; useful against noise but risky if it hides real attacks.
Tampering with the data a model learns from, so it learns to ignore or mislabel certain activity.
A design in which a person reviews or approves important automated decisions before they take effect.

subtopics.name: Threat Actors and Motives
subtopics.definition: A threat actor is a person or group that could harm an organization's systems or data; knowing their motive, such as money, spying or protest, predicts what they target.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Different actors want different things and have very different skills. Knowing who is likely to target the organization, and why, helps defenders focus on the attacks that are most likely and most damaging.
how_it_works: Actors differ in motive, skill, resources and whether they are inside or outside the organization.
Motive predicts the target: criminals seek payment data or ransom, spies seek secrets, and activists seek publicity or embarrassment.
Advanced persistent threats are skilled, well-funded groups, often state-linked, that stay hidden in a network for long periods.
Insiders already have access; some act with intent, but many cause harm through mistakes, such as misdirected emails.
Low-skill attackers use ready-made tools, yet still succeed against unpatched systems and weak passwords.

types.meaning: Government-linked groups, usually seeking espionage or disruption, with the most skill and resources.
Groups seeking money through ransomware, fraud and selling stolen data.
Attackers driven by a political or social cause, often using defacement, leaks or denial of service.
Current or former staff, contractors or partners who misuse their access, deliberately or by accident.
Someone with little expertise using ready-made tools, often for thrills or notoriety.
A rival organization seeking trade secrets or advantage through industrial espionage.

subtopics.example: A small engineering firm wins a government contract to design a bridge component. Soon after, staff receive well-written emails that seem to come from the client, asking them to open design 'revisions'. Rowan, the firm's only security analyst, notes that the target and the patience fit an espionage-minded actor more than a quick fraud, reports the pattern to the IT manager and suggests a phishing warning to all staff.

review: Note the likely motive when you write up suspicious activity
Share relevant sector threat reports with your team when policy allows
evidence: Which assets attackers with each motive would most want
Signs of insider misuse, such as unusual downloads before someone leaves
audit_focus.recommend: Report suspected insider activity quietly to your supervisor or the security lead, not to the person or coworkers.
audit_focus.decides: Management, with human resources and legal counsel, decides actions on suspected insiders

subtopics.isaca_rule: Ask who would want this and why. Motive points to the likely target and method, which tells defenders what to protect first. Never assume the organization is too small to target: criminals and automated attacks hit everyone.

exam_traps.trap: Insider threats are always malicious employees.
exam_traps.why: Many insider incidents are mistakes, such as sending data to the wrong person or falling for phishing. Training and controls aim at both careless and malicious insiders.

exam_traps.trap: Only nation-states are dangerous, so small organizations need not worry.
exam_traps.why: Criminal groups and automated tools attack any organization with weak defenses, and small firms are often stepping stones into larger partners.

key_terms.definition: A skilled, well-resourced attacker that gains access and stays hidden for a long time to reach its goal.
The path or method an attacker uses to reach a target, such as email, a web application or a USB drive.

subtopics.name: Cyber Threat Intelligence
subtopics.definition: Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) is information about threats that has been collected, analyzed and put in context, so defenders can make better decisions about likely attacks.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Raw threat data, such as lists of bad Internet Protocol (IP) addresses, is noise until someone judges what matters here. Good intelligence says which threats to expect, how they operate and what to look for.
how_it_works: Intelligence comes from open sources, vendors, government agencies and sector sharing groups such as Information Sharing and Analysis Centers (ISACs).
Indicators of compromise, such as malicious file hashes, domains or IP addresses, are fed into tools to block or detect known threats.
Indicators go stale quickly because attackers change infrastructure, so intelligence about attacker methods stays useful longer.
The intelligence cycle runs from defining what the organization needs, through collection and analysis, to sharing results and gathering feedback.
Shared intelligence carries a Traffic Light Protocol (TLP) label, such as TLP:RED or TLP:CLEAR, saying how far it may be passed on.

types.meaning: High-level trends and risks for leaders, such as which actors target the sector and why.
Details of specific campaigns, such as who is targeting the organization now and how.
Attacker tactics, techniques and procedures, used to shape defenses and detections.
Specific indicators, such as hashes and addresses, used directly by security tools.

subtopics.example: A water utility's sector ISAC shares a TLP:AMBER report on ransomware hitting other utilities through an unpatched remote access appliance, with indicators attached. Noor, a junior analyst, searches the utility's logs for the indicators and confirms the same appliance model is in use. Noor shares the report only with the internal team the label allows and gives the findings to the security manager.

review: Search your logs and tools for indicators from new trusted reports
Keep the original TLP label on any intelligence you pass on
evidence: Whether products named in reports appear in your asset inventory
The age and source of indicators before blocking on them
audit_focus.recommend: Send intelligence that matches your environment to the security manager or incident response lead promptly.
audit_focus.decides: The security manager decides what to block and which systems to prioritize

subtopics.isaca_rule: Intelligence helps only when it is relevant, timely and acted on. Check it against your own assets, feed indicators to your tools, and respect sharing labels such as TLP, or the sharing community stops trusting you.

exam_traps.trap: More threat feeds always mean better security.
exam_traps.why: Unfiltered feeds add noise and false positives. Value comes from intelligence that matches the organization's sector and assets, and that someone acts on.

exam_traps.trap: A TLP:AMBER report can be posted to a public forum to warn others.
exam_traps.why: AMBER limits sharing to the recipient's organization, and its clients where they need to know. Only TLP:CLEAR information may be shared publicly.

key_terms.definition: Evidence that a system may have been breached, such as a known malicious file hash, domain or address.
A labeling standard from the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST) that sets how widely shared information may travel.

subtopics.name: Threat Frameworks: MITRE ATT&CK and the Kill Chain
subtopics.definition: Threat frameworks describe how attacks unfold in a shared language; MITRE ATT&CK catalogs real attacker goals and methods, while the Cyber Kill Chain sets out attack stages in order.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A common language lets analysts, tools and intelligence reports describe the same behavior the same way. Mapping defenses to a framework shows what the organization can detect and where the gaps are.
how_it_works: ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) is a free knowledge base from the nonprofit MITRE, built from observed attacks rather than theory.
Tactics are the attacker's goals, such as initial access or exfiltration; techniques are the ways each goal is reached, such as phishing.
Defenders map their detections to techniques to find gaps, and red teams use the same map to plan realistic tests.
The Cyber Kill Chain, from Lockheed Martin, has seven stages, from reconnaissance to actions on objectives; breaking any link can stop the attack.

rows.label: Shape
cells: A matrix of tactics, each with many techniques
Seven stages in a fixed order

rows.label: Built from
cells: A model of how intrusions progress

rows.label: Best for
cells: Mapping detections and gaps in detail
Explaining an attack's flow and where to break it

rows.label: Limit
cells: Large; not a checklist to complete
Less detail; fits outside intrusions best

subtopics.example: After a phishing incident, a museum's security lead asks Quinn, a junior analyst, to map it to ATT&CK. Quinn lists each step against its tactic: the phishing email (initial access), a malicious macro (execution), a scheduled task restarting the malware (persistence) and a large upload to a file-sharing site (exfiltration). Quinn marks which steps raised alerts, giving the lead a list of detection gaps.

review: Tag alerts and incident notes with the matching ATT&CK technique
List which steps of a past attack were and were not detected
evidence: Coverage of techniques used by actors targeting your sector
Techniques that raised no alert during tests
audit_focus.recommend: Share the detection gaps you find with the security operations lead, with the evidence behind each one.
audit_focus.decides: The security operations lead or security manager decides which gaps to close first

subtopics.isaca_rule: Frameworks are maps, not checklists. Use them to describe attacks, find detection gaps and plan tests. Nobody needs to cover every technique; focus on those the likely attackers actually use.

exam_traps.trap: MITRE ATT&CK is a compliance standard that an organization must fully implement.
exam_traps.why: ATT&CK is a knowledge base of attacker behavior, not a set of required controls. Organizations use it selectively to guide detection and testing.

exam_traps.trap: Tactics and techniques mean the same thing.
exam_traps.why: A tactic is the attacker's goal, the why; a technique is the method used to reach it, the how. One tactic has many techniques.

key_terms.definition: How an attacker operates: the goals (tactics), the methods (techniques) and a group's specific way of doing them (procedures).
A companion knowledge base (Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems) describing attacks on artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning.
Which attacker techniques monitoring can actually spot, often shown as a heat map over ATT&CK.

topics.overview: Incident response is how an organization prepares for, detects, contains and recovers from incidents, then learns from them. This topic covers the incident response plan and team, the lifecycle in NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, and its link to the Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0, handling evidence and data during a response, and testing the plan with exercises such as tabletops.
can_do: Put the incident response phases in order, and explain why containment comes before eradication
Map the classic lifecycle phases to the CSF 2.0 functions used in NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3
Preserve evidence and keep a chain of custody while following the data handling policy
Choose the right exercise, such as a tabletop, to test an incident response plan

subtopics.name: The Incident Response Plan and Team
subtopics.definition: An incident response plan is the approved document that says what counts as an incident, who responds, what authority they have, how to communicate, and which steps to follow.
subtopics.why_it_matters: In a crisis, people improvise, act alone or wait for permission. A plan approved in advance by management sets roles, authority and contacts, so the response is fast, lawful and coordinated.
how_it_works: Senior management approves the plan, which gives the incident response team authority to act, such as isolating systems.
Severity levels set how fast to respond and who must be told, with clear escalation thresholds.
Playbooks give step-by-step actions for common incidents, such as ransomware, phishing and lost devices.
Contact lists are kept current, including after-hours numbers, outside partners and an out-of-band channel in case email is compromised.
Everyone, not just the team, knows how to report a suspected incident, and the plan is reviewed after major incidents and changes.

types.meaning: Coordinates the response, makes operational decisions and keeps management informed.
Investigate, contain and eradicate the threat, and preserve evidence.
Advises on laws, contracts, evidence and notification duties.
Prepares approved messages for staff, customers, regulators and the media.
Approves major business decisions, such as shutting down a service or paying for outside help.

subtopics.example: Late on a Friday, Sky, an IT technician at a community college, sees ransom notes appearing on a shared drive. Sky's instinct is to start restoring files, but the plan's first step for staff is to report through the on-call number. Sky calls it, describes what they saw and when, and keeps notes while waiting for the incident lead to direct the response.

review: Know the reporting number and channel before you ever need them
Report suspected incidents immediately, with what you saw and when
evidence: The current contact list and on-call schedule
Which playbook fits the situation you have found
audit_focus.recommend: Report anything that may be an incident to the incident response team through the plan's channel, even when unsure.
audit_focus.decides: The incident lead directs the response; management approves major business decisions

subtopics.isaca_rule: Follow the plan, use the defined reporting path, and act only within your role. The plan exists so nobody has to improvise or decide alone in a crisis; escalate early and let the incident lead coordinate.

exam_traps.trap: An experienced technician should fix an incident quietly to avoid alarming management.
exam_traps.why: Quiet fixes skip evidence collection, notification duties and coordination. Report through the plan's path so the right people can decide.

exam_traps.trap: Email is the best way to coordinate the response team.
exam_traps.why: If the attacker controls email or the network, they can read the response plan as it unfolds. The plan should name an out-of-band channel.

key_terms.definition: Contact through a separate channel, such as phones, that an attacker inside the main network cannot read.
A defined trigger, such as data loss or a critical system down, that requires telling a higher level.
The group responsible for handling incidents; it may be in-house, outsourced or a mix.

subtopics.name: The Incident Response Lifecycle and CSF 2.0
subtopics.definition: The incident response lifecycle runs from preparation through detection and analysis, containment, eradication and recovery to lessons learned, which feed back into preparation.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Steps done out of order cause harm: wiping a machine before containment lets the attacker carry on elsewhere, and restoring before eradication brings the attacker back.
how_it_works: Preparation builds the plan, team, tools and training before anything happens.
Detection and analysis confirm an incident, judge its scope and severity, and start the record.
Containment stops the spread, eradication removes the cause, and recovery restores normal operations from known-good sources while watching for a return.
Lessons learned review what happened and feed improvements back into the plan and controls.
The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) SP 800-61 Rev. 3 maps this work to the six Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 functions, with improvement running continuously.

rows.label: Improve
cells: Identify's improvement category, at any time

subtopics.example: Malware is found on a ferry company's ticketing server, and a sales manager wants it rebuilt from the latest backup at once. Ellis, a systems administrator on the response team, raises the plan's order with the incident lead: isolate the server and check other systems first, remove the cause and confirm the backup predates the infection, and only then restore. The lead agrees.

review: Check which phase the response is in before taking an action
Log each action with time, system and reason as you go
evidence: Scope of affected systems before anything is wiped or restored
Backup dates compared with the first sign of compromise
audit_focus.recommend: Raise pressure to skip a phase, such as restoring before eradication, with the incident lead.
audit_focus.decides: The incident lead decides when to move between phases

subtopics.isaca_rule: Order matters: contain before you eradicate, eradicate before you recover, and learn from every incident. Whichever model the organization uses, the classic phases and the CSF 2.0 functions describe the same work.

exam_traps.trap: The first thing to do when malware is found is to wipe and rebuild the machine.
exam_traps.why: Wiping first destroys evidence and does nothing about other infected systems. Contain and scope the incident first, then eradicate and recover.

exam_traps.trap: Under SP 800-61 Rev. 3, lessons are gathered only after the incident is closed.
exam_traps.why: Rev. 3 treats improvement as continuous: lessons can be captured and shared as soon as they are found, not held for a final review.

key_terms.definition: The NIST framework, published in 2024, organized into six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.
NIST's April 2025 incident response guidance, written as a CSF 2.0 profile; it replaced Rev. 2 from 2012.
The CSF 2.0 category for finding improvements from incidents, exercises and daily work.

subtopics.memory_aid: Prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover, learn: stop it before you scrub it.

subtopics.name: Containment, Eradication and Recovery
subtopics.definition: Containment stops an incident from spreading, eradication removes its cause, and recovery returns affected systems to normal, trusted operation, in that order.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Cleaning up before containing lets an attacker move to other systems or destroy data. Restoring before the cause is removed puts the same weakness, or the attacker, straight back into production.
how_it_works: Short-term containment acts fast, for example isolating an infected laptop from the network or disabling a compromised account.
Isolating a running machine, rather than powering it off, usually keeps memory evidence; the playbook may say otherwise for some threats.
Eradication removes malware and attacker accounts, closes the exploited weakness and resets exposed credentials on every affected system.
Recovery restores from known-good backups or clean builds, patches and hardens them, then monitors closely for signs of return.
subtopics.example: At a dental practice group, an office manager reports pop-ups and locked files on a reception PC. Robin, the IT support technician, follows the ransomware playbook: they unplug the PC's network cable but leave it powered on, disable the user's account through the approved process, and call the incident lead. Robin runs no cleanup tools and restores nothing until the lead confirms the scope.

review: Isolate the affected system as the playbook directs, leaving it running
Reset or disable exposed credentials only as the incident lead directs
evidence: Other systems showing the same indicators
Backup dates against the earliest sign of compromise
audit_focus.recommend: Hand over to the incident lead before running cleanup tools, wiping or restoring anything.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner, advised by the incident lead, approves the return to service

subtopics.isaca_rule: Contain first, then eradicate, then recover. Isolate rather than power off unless the playbook says otherwise, remove every trace of the cause before restoring, and restore only from sources known to be clean.

exam_traps.trap: Powering off an infected computer is the safest first step.
exam_traps.why: Powering off can erase memory evidence, such as running malware and open connections. Isolating it from the network usually stops the spread and keeps evidence. Follow the playbook.

exam_traps.trap: Once malware is removed from the first infected laptop, the incident is over.
exam_traps.why: Attackers often spread or leave persistence on other systems. Eradication covers every affected system and the original weakness, or the incident returns.

key_terms.definition: Cutting a system off from the network, by cable or with endpoint tools, while leaving it running.
A backup taken before the compromise and confirmed clean, so restoring it does not bring the threat back.
Methods an attacker uses to keep access after a reboot or cleanup, such as hidden accounts or scheduled tasks.

subtopics.name: Evidence Handling and Chain of Custody
subtopics.definition: Evidence handling preserves digital and physical evidence so it stays reliable, and chain of custody records everyone who handled it, when and why, from collection onward.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An incident may lead to disciplinary action, insurance claims or court. Evidence that was altered, or that cannot be shown to be untouched, may be rejected, and the facts may never be proven.
how_it_works: The most volatile evidence, such as memory and network connections, is collected before disk contents that survive a shutdown.
Investigators work on verified copies, called forensic images, and keep the original sealed and unchanged.
A hash of the evidence is taken at collection; a matching hash later shows nothing has changed.
Every transfer is logged with date, time, names, purpose and storage location, and evidence is locked away with restricted access.
Entry-level staff preserve the scene and report; trained forensic staff, often guided by legal counsel, collect and analyze.
subtopics.example: A warehouse supervisor finds an unfamiliar USB drive plugged into the back of a payroll PC. Pat, a security technician, photographs the PC and drive in place, does not open any files, and calls the incident lead. When the forensic investigator arrives, Pat hands over the photos and notes, and the investigator records the collection, including Pat's part, on the chain of custody form.

review: Leave the device as found and note its state, time and location
Record every action you take on affected systems
evidence: Custody records with a name, time and reason for every handoff
Hash values recorded at collection and at each analysis
audit_focus.recommend: Call the incident lead before touching suspected evidence, and let trained forensic staff collect it.
audit_focus.decides: Legal counsel and the incident lead decide how evidence is collected and kept

subtopics.isaca_rule: Preserve first, analyze later, and only within your role. Do not browse, copy or clean a suspect device. Write down what you saw and did, and make sure every handoff of evidence is recorded.

exam_traps.trap: The analyst should open the suspicious files right away to see what they contain.
exam_traps.why: Opening files changes timestamps and may run malware, damaging both the evidence and the network. Preserve the device and let trained staff analyze a forensic copy.

exam_traps.trap: Chain of custody matters only if the police are already involved.
exam_traps.why: Many incidents become legal or disciplinary cases later. If custody was not recorded from the start, it cannot be rebuilt afterward.

key_terms.definition: Collecting the evidence that disappears fastest first, such as memory, then disk, then backups.
An exact bit-for-bit copy of storage media, verified by hash, analyzed instead of the original.
A device or tool that lets investigators read a drive without changing any data on it.

subtopics.name: Data Handling During an Incident
subtopics.definition: Data handling during an incident means applying the organization's classification and handling rules to everything the response touches, including evidence, logs, reports and communications.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Responders copy disk images, logs and customer records, which can hold the very data the attacker wanted. Mishandling those copies, or saying too much too soon, can turn one incident into a second breach or a legal problem.
how_it_works: Evidence and incident reports take the classification of the most sensitive data they contain, and are stored and shared by those rules.
Details are shared on a need-to-know basis through approved secure channels, not personal email or chat apps.
The incident record notes which data types were affected, such as personal or payment data, because that drives legal duties.
Only designated roles, such as communications and legal counsel, speak to customers, regulators or the media.
Notification deadlines vary by law and contract, so the incident lead involves legal counsel early.
subtopics.example: During a suspected data theft at a travel agency, a reporter calls the front desk asking whether customer passport details were exposed. A colleague asks Leah, a junior analyst helping the response, to 'just tell them it isn't true'. Leah declines, takes the reporter's details for the communications lead as the plan requires, and keeps working only in the incident's restricted case folder.

review: Store incident files only in the approved restricted case location
Refer outside questions to the designated spokesperson
evidence: Data types and classification levels the incident involves
Access lists on the case folder, limited to named responders
audit_focus.recommend: Tell the incident lead at once if you learn that personal, health or payment data may be involved.
audit_focus.decides: Legal counsel and management decide notifications and public statements

subtopics.isaca_rule: During a response, handling rules get stricter, not looser. Keep incident data in approved restricted locations, share on a need-to-know basis, and leave statements and notifications to the roles the plan names.

exam_traps.trap: In an emergency, it is fine to send logs to a personal email account to keep working from home.
exam_traps.why: Logs and evidence can hold sensitive data. Sending them outside approved systems creates a new exposure and breaks the handling policy, emergency or not.

exam_traps.trap: A responder who knows the facts should reassure customers directly.
exam_traps.why: Early statements may be wrong and can create legal risk. The plan names who speaks for the organization; refer questions to them.

key_terms.definition: Sharing information only with people who require it to do their part in the response.
A legal or contractual duty to tell affected people, regulators or partners about certain breaches within set deadlines.
The person authorized to speak for the organization about an incident; everyone else refers questions to them.

subtopics.name: Lessons Learned and Continuous Improvement
subtopics.definition: Lessons learned is the review after an incident or exercise that asks what happened, what worked, what did not and what to change, then tracks those changes to completion.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without a review, the same weakness causes the next incident. Improvements are also how the plan stays current as systems, threats and people change.
how_it_works: The review happens soon after the incident, while memories are fresh, and includes everyone who took part.
It is blameless: it looks for gaps in process, tools and training rather than someone to punish, so people speak openly.
Findings become actions with owners and deadlines, such as updating a playbook, adding a detection or fixing a control.
NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 treats improvement as continuous, so lessons can be shared during the incident, not only at the end.
Measures such as time to detect and time to contain show whether the changes are working.
subtopics.example: Two weeks after a phishing attack at a nonprofit, the incident lead holds a review. Drew, the help desk technician, explains that three staff called the help desk about the strange email an hour before anyone told security, because help desk scripts had no reporting step. The group adds a 'forward to security' step to the scripts, with Drew's manager as the owner.

review: Bring your timeline notes and observations to the review
Complete improvement actions assigned to you and report progress
evidence: Open improvement actions and their due dates
Whether the same root cause appeared in earlier incidents
audit_focus.recommend: Raise overdue or unowned improvement actions with the incident lead or your manager.
audit_focus.decides: Management approves and funds the improvements

subtopics.isaca_rule: Every incident and exercise should change something. Speak up honestly in reviews, focus on process rather than blame, and make sure each improvement has an owner and a due date.

exam_traps.trap: The main goal of the review is to find out who was at fault.
exam_traps.why: Blame makes people hide mistakes and early warnings. Reviews look for process and control gaps so the organization improves.

exam_traps.trap: A small incident does not need a lessons learned review.
exam_traps.why: Small incidents often reveal the same gaps as big ones, at lower cost. The plan sets how deep the review goes, but some review always adds value.

key_terms.definition: A written summary of an incident or exercise: its timeline, findings and agreed improvement actions.
The underlying reason an incident happened, such as a missing patch, rather than its symptoms.
The average time between an incident starting and the organization noticing it.

subtopics.name: Incident Response Exercises and Tabletops
subtopics.definition: Incident response exercises test the plan and the people before a real incident, ranging from discussion-based tabletops to hands-on simulations and full-scale exercises.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A plan nobody has practiced fails under pressure: phone numbers are wrong, roles are unclear and decisions stall. Exercises find these gaps while mistakes cost nothing.
how_it_works: Each exercise has clear objectives, a realistic scenario and an agreed scope, so it does not disrupt real operations.
A facilitator presents the scenario in stages, adding new facts called injects to test decisions as the situation changes.
Observers note what worked and what did not, and the exercise ends with a debrief and an after-action report.
Findings feed lessons learned, such as updated contacts, clearer roles, new playbooks or extra training.
Exercises repeat regularly and after major changes, and can include outside parties such as cloud providers, legal counsel and insurers.

types.meaning: A discussion-based session where the team talks through its response to a scenario; no systems are touched.
A focused practice of one task, such as calling the contact list or isolating a test laptop.
Teams carry out their roles in a simulated environment, under realistic time pressure, without touching production.
Many teams, and sometimes outside partners, respond to a realistic scenario as close to real operations as is safe.

subtopics.example: A food distribution company runs its first ransomware tabletop. Halfway through, the facilitator adds an inject: the email system is down. The team realizes nobody has the incident lead's mobile number and the contact list exists only in email. Mika, the junior analyst taking notes, records the gap, and after the debrief it becomes an action to keep a printed, offline contact list.

review: Play the role you would hold in a real incident
Note anything unclear in your instructions or contacts
evidence: Your assigned role and the contact list you would use
After-action items assigned to your team
audit_focus.recommend: Report gaps you notice during an exercise to the facilitator or exercise lead, even if they seem minor.
audit_focus.decides: Management sets the exercise schedule and approves the resulting changes

subtopics.isaca_rule: Practice before you need it. Start with tabletops to check roles and decisions, move to hands-on exercises as the plan matures, and treat every gap found as a success to fix, not a failure to hide.

exam_traps.trap: A tabletop exercise proves that systems can actually be restored.
exam_traps.why: Tabletops are discussions; they test understanding, roles and decisions. Proving technical recovery needs a hands-on test, such as a functional exercise or a restore test.

exam_traps.trap: An exercise is needed only once, when the plan is first written.
exam_traps.why: People, systems and threats change. Exercises repeat regularly and after major changes to keep the plan workable.

key_terms.definition: A new piece of scenario information introduced during an exercise to test how the team adapts.
The person who runs an exercise, presents the scenario and keeps discussion on its objectives.

topics.overview: You cannot protect what you do not know you have. This topic covers keeping an inventory of hardware, software, data, cloud and AI assets with named owners, managing each asset from purchase to disposal, handling end-of-life systems, and keeping systems in a secure, known state through configuration, patch and change management.
can_do: Explain why an accurate asset inventory with named owners comes first
Choose a safe option for end-of-life software or devices that can no longer be patched
Describe secure baselines, configuration drift and how patches are prioritized and tested
Follow the change management steps, including for emergency changes

subtopics.name: Asset Inventory and Ownership
subtopics.definition: An asset inventory is an up-to-date list of the organization's hardware, software, data, cloud services and artificial intelligence (AI) assets, each with a named owner responsible for it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Unknown assets are not patched, monitored or backed up, so attackers often get in through them. The inventory is the starting point for nearly every other control.
how_it_works: Automated discovery tools scan networks and cloud accounts for devices and services, and the results are matched against purchase records.
Each entry records the owner, location, criticality, data handled and support status, so risks can be ranked.
Software inventories list approved applications and versions, so unapproved or vulnerable software stands out.
AI assets include models, training data sets, prompts and outside AI services, which are tracked like any other asset.
Unknown devices or services found on the network are investigated, then brought under management or removed through procedure.
subtopics.example: A network scan at an elementary school finds a device nobody recognizes: a video recorder for the old security cameras, still using its factory password. Jesse, the school's IT technician, adds it to the inventory, asks the facilities manager to confirm they own it, and logs the default password as a finding for the owner to fix through the change process.

review: Add new assets to the inventory before or as they are deployed
Investigate unknown devices that discovery scans find
evidence: Discovery results compared with the inventory for unlisted assets
Inventory entries missing an owner or a support end date
audit_focus.recommend: Report unknown or unowned assets to your supervisor so that an owner can be assigned.
audit_focus.decides: The asset owner decides how the asset is used and accepts its risks

subtopics.isaca_rule: Inventory comes first: every asset needs an entry and an owner. When you find something unknown, record it and find its owner instead of ignoring it or unplugging it on your own.

exam_traps.trap: Whoever finds an unknown device on the network should unplug it immediately.
exam_traps.why: It may support a business process, such as cameras or medical equipment. Report it and follow procedure; isolate it at once only if it is actively harmful and the procedure allows.

exam_traps.trap: The asset inventory needs to list only hardware.
exam_traps.why: Software, data, cloud services and AI models are assets too. Each can be attacked and needs an owner and protection.

key_terms.definition: The person accountable for an asset's protection and use, who approves access and accepts its risks.
Technology used for work without IT or security approval, such as unapproved cloud apps or personal devices.
A central record of assets, their configurations and how they connect, used in change and incident work.

subtopics.name: The Asset Lifecycle
subtopics.definition: The asset lifecycle covers each stage of an asset's life, from planning and buying through deployment, operation and maintenance to retirement and secure disposal.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Security problems are cheapest to avoid early and easiest to forget at the end. A device bought without security requirements, or thrown out without sanitization, can expose data long after anyone remembers it.
how_it_works: Planning and acquisition set security requirements, such as encryption support and vendor patch commitments, before anything is bought.
Deployment applies the secure baseline, records the asset in the inventory and assigns its owner.
Operation and maintenance keep the asset, including artificial intelligence (AI) tools and their models, patched, monitored and backed up, with changes made through change management.
Retirement takes the asset out of service and removes it from access lists, firewall rules and monitoring.
Disposal sanitizes or destroys storage, records the result and updates the inventory, including for leased or returned equipment.
subtopics.example: A grocery chain replaces its warehouse handheld scanners, and the old units are boxed for a recycler. Kim, an IT technician, notices the scanners still hold cached delivery addresses and saved Wi-Fi passwords. Kim pauses the shipment, tells the asset manager, sanitizes each device and records its serial number as the disposal procedure requires, and asks the network team to change the Wi-Fi password.

review: Follow the disposal procedure for every retired device, including small ones
Remove retired assets from monitoring, access lists and the inventory
evidence: Disposal records matched against assets marked as retired
Leased or returned equipment still waiting for sanitization
