audit_focus.recommend: Report any asset about to leave the organization without sanitization records to the asset manager.
audit_focus.decides: The asset owner approves retirement; policy sets the disposal method

subtopics.isaca_rule: Security belongs at every stage, not only while an asset is in use. Build requirements in before purchase, and close out properly at the end: sanitize, update the records and remove access.

exam_traps.trap: Security starts once a system is installed.
exam_traps.why: Requirements set at purchase decide whether the product can be secured and patched at all. Fixing a poor choice after deployment costs far more.

exam_traps.trap: A retired server can stay switched off in the rack until someone has time to deal with it.
exam_traps.why: Retired assets still hold data and may still have accounts and network access. Decommission and dispose of them through the process.

key_terms.definition: Conditions a product or service must meet before purchase, such as patch support, encryption and logging.
Formally taking an asset out of service, including removing its accounts, network access and monitoring entries.
Ending an asset's life so no data can be recovered, using sanitization or destruction, with records kept.

subtopics.name: End-of-Life Software and Devices
subtopics.definition: End-of-life (EOL) software or hardware no longer gets vendor support, including security patches, so newly found weaknesses stay unfixed for good.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Attackers look for unsupported products because every new flaw becomes permanent. EOL systems often run important processes, so they need a plan long before support ends, not after.
how_it_works: Vendors usually announce end-of-sale, end-of-support and end-of-life dates in advance; for security, the key date is when patches stop.
The inventory tracks support dates, so owners can plan upgrades and budgets before the deadline.
The preferred fix is to upgrade or replace the system before support ends.
If that is not yet possible, reduce exposure: isolate the system on its own network segment, limit access, monitor it closely, or buy extended support.
Any EOL system kept in use is recorded as a risk exception, with the owner's acceptance and a review date.
subtopics.example: A medical clinic's ultrasound machine runs an operating system that lost vendor support last year, and its maker will not approve an upgrade for two more years. Ari, a junior network administrator, records the machine as end-of-life, proposes moving it to an isolated network segment reachable only from the imaging workstation, and sends the proposal to the owner, the clinic manager, for a decision and a formal risk exception.

review: Flag assets whose support ends within the next year
Propose compensating controls when an EOL system cannot be replaced yet
evidence: Support status and end dates in the asset inventory
Risk exceptions for EOL systems and their review dates
audit_focus.recommend: Send EOL findings to the asset owner and security manager, with the support end date and the data at risk.
audit_focus.decides: The asset owner accepts the risk or funds the upgrade

subtopics.isaca_rule: Plan for end of support before it arrives. Upgrade or replace when you can; when you cannot, isolate, restrict and monitor, and get the owner's documented risk acceptance. Never let an unsupported system quietly stay as it is.

exam_traps.trap: If an unsupported system still works, it is safe to leave as is.
exam_traps.why: Working is not the same as secure. Every flaw found after support ends stays open, so the system needs replacing or compensating controls.

exam_traps.trap: An analyst should switch off an unsupported machine as soon as they find it.
exam_traps.why: It may run a critical or life-safety process. Report it to the owner, who decides with security on replacement or compensating controls.

key_terms.definition: The date after which a vendor stops fixing problems, including security flaws, in a product version.
An alternative safeguard, such as network isolation, used when the normal control, such as patching, is not possible.
A documented, time-limited approval to operate outside a policy, with the owner accepting the remaining risk.

subtopics.name: Configuration Management and Secure Baselines
subtopics.definition: Configuration management keeps systems in a known, approved state by defining secure baselines, applying them consistently, and detecting and correcting drift away from them.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Default settings are built for easy setup, not security, and attackers know them well. Without baselines, every system ends up configured differently, so weaknesses are easy to miss and hard to fix.
how_it_works: A secure baseline is the approved minimum configuration for one type of system, such as a laptop, web server, firewall or artificial intelligence (AI) service.
Hardening removes what is not needed, such as unused services, ports, accounts and software, and changes default passwords and settings.
Organizations often start from published guides such as the Center for Internet Security (CIS) Benchmarks, then adapt them to their needs.
Automated tools apply the baseline to new systems and scan existing ones for drift, such as a disabled firewall or a new local administrator.
Drift is corrected or approved as a documented change, and the baseline itself is updated only through change management.
subtopics.example: A monthly scan at a housing association shows twelve laptops with full-disk encryption turned off, against the baseline. Fran, a desktop support technician, finds that a contractor disabled it to speed up a software install and never turned it back on. Fran opens a ticket, re-enables encryption with the approved tool, and reports the cause to the desktop team lead so the install process can be fixed.

review: Build new systems from the approved baseline image or template
Return drifted settings to the baseline with approved tools
evidence: Drift scan results against the current baseline
Hardening checklist results for each new build
audit_focus.recommend: Report repeated drift, or a baseline setting that blocks business work, to your team lead for a formal change.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner and the security team approve the baseline

subtopics.isaca_rule: Start every system from an approved baseline and treat any difference as a question: is it an approved change or drift? Return drift to the baseline, and change the baseline itself only through change management.

exam_traps.trap: Default settings from a reputable vendor are secure enough to deploy.
exam_traps.why: Defaults favor easy setup and are publicly known, including default passwords. Systems are hardened to a baseline before they go live.

exam_traps.trap: A system that passed the baseline check at deployment stays compliant.
exam_traps.why: Updates, troubleshooting and quick fixes cause drift over time. Regular scans compare systems with the baseline to catch it.

key_terms.definition: Reducing a system's attack surface by removing unneeded features and tightening its settings.
Gradual, often unapproved changes that move a system away from its approved baseline.
Free, consensus-based secure configuration guides for common systems, published by the Center for Internet Security.

subtopics.name: Patch Management
subtopics.definition: Patch management finds, tests, approves and installs software updates that fix security flaws and bugs, then confirms they worked, across every system in the inventory.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Many breaches use flaws that already had a patch available. Patching quickly closes those doors, but careless patching can break critical systems, so speed and testing must be balanced.
how_it_works: Teams watch vendor notices and vulnerability scan results to learn which systems need which patches.
Patches are prioritized by risk: the flaw's severity, whether attackers are exploiting it, and how exposed and critical the system is.
Patches are tested on non-production systems first, then deployed through the change process with a rollback plan.
Urgent patches for actively exploited flaws use the emergency change route, which is faster but still recorded.
Rescans or reports confirm each patch installed; systems that cannot be patched get compensating controls and an exception.
subtopics.example: A vendor releases a fix for a flaw in a file transfer product that attackers are already exploiting, and a pharmacy chain runs the product on an internet-facing server. Devon, a systems administrator, checks the inventory, confirms the server is affected and raises an emergency change. After a quick test on the standby server and approval from the change manager, Devon applies the patch and rescans to confirm it.

review: Check affected systems against the inventory when a patch is released
Confirm installation with a rescan after deployment
evidence: Patch compliance reports showing missing patches by system
Whether a flaw appears on an exploited-vulnerabilities list
audit_focus.recommend: Raise any actively exploited flaw on an exposed system with your team lead the same day.
audit_focus.decides: The change manager or change advisory board approves deployment

subtopics.isaca_rule: Patch by risk, not by habit: actively exploited flaws on exposed, critical systems come first. Test, use the change process, even its emergency route, and verify. If you cannot patch, protect and document.

exam_traps.trap: Install every patch on production systems the moment it is released.
exam_traps.why: Untested patches can break critical services. Test first, and use the emergency change process when the risk demands speed.

exam_traps.trap: Patches can wait for the quarterly cycle, whatever the flaw.
exam_traps.why: Actively exploited flaws on exposed systems need fast action. Priority depends on risk, not on a fixed calendar.

key_terms.definition: A public list, kept by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, of flaws confirmed as exploited in real attacks.
A flaw that attackers exploit before the vendor has released a fix.
An agreed time for planned changes, such as patching, when disruption to users is lowest.

subtopics.name: Change Management
subtopics.definition: Change management is the controlled process for requesting, assessing, approving, testing, carrying out and reviewing changes to systems, so changes do not cause outages or security gaps.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Unplanned and untested changes are a leading cause of outages, and an unapproved change can quietly open a security hole. A record of approved changes also helps responders spot what is not normal.
how_it_works: A change request describes what will change and why, the risk and impact, the test plan and the rollback plan.
An approver reviews the request; the person making the change does not approve their own work.
Approved changes are tested, scheduled, carried out and checked, and configuration records are updated.
Emergency changes can be approved quickly by a designated person, but are recorded and reviewed soon afterward.
Changes found without approval are treated as possible incidents until they are explained.
subtopics.example: A finance manager at a construction firm asks Jo, a network technician, to open a firewall port right away so a supplier can upload invoices. Jo sees the need is real but there is no approval. Jo raises a change request describing the port, the supplier's addresses and a rollback plan, and tells the manager the change approver can fast-track it if the need is urgent.

review: Raise a change request before changing any production system
Wait for recorded approval before starting, even under pressure
evidence: The change calendar for conflicts before scheduling work
Unapproved changes found in configuration or drift reports
audit_focus.recommend: Report pressure to make an unapproved change, or an unexplained change you find, to your supervisor or the change manager.
audit_focus.decides: The change advisory board or designated approver authorizes the change

subtopics.isaca_rule: No change without approval, testing and a way back. Urgency changes how fast approval happens, not whether it happens. Keep the person who requests or makes a change separate from the person who approves it.

exam_traps.trap: Emergency changes skip the change process entirely.
exam_traps.why: They use a faster route with a designated approver, but they are still recorded and reviewed afterward. Skipping the process leaves no record and no check.

exam_traps.trap: A small configuration change by a senior engineer needs no approval.
exam_traps.why: Small changes can cause big outages or security gaps. Seniority does not replace review, testing and a rollback plan.

key_terms.definition: A group that reviews and approves significant changes, weighing business, technical and security impact.
Steps prepared in advance to undo a change if it fails or causes problems.
A change that must happen faster than the normal process allows, approved quickly and reviewed afterward.

topics.overview: Security testing checks whether defenses work before an attacker finds out they do not. This topic covers red, blue and purple teams, vulnerability scanning and penetration testing, application testing with static and dynamic analysis, threat modeling, physical and social engineering tests, and testing defenses that rely on AI. Every test needs written authorization and an agreed scope.
can_do: Tell a vulnerability scan from a penetration test, and tell red, blue and purple teams apart
Explain where static analysis, dynamic analysis and threat modeling fit in development
Describe phishing, tailgating and impersonation tests and the authorization each needs
Explain how to test a defense that relies on AI, including against prompt injection

subtopics.name: Red, Blue and Purple Teams
subtopics.definition: A red team plays the attacker, a blue team defends and detects, and a purple team is red and blue working together to improve detection and response.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Defenses that are never challenged give false confidence. Testing with realistic attacks shows whether people, processes and tools actually detect and stop what real attackers do.
how_it_works: Red teams emulate real threat actors, often using MITRE ATT&CK techniques, to reach agreed goals, such as reading a test file in the payroll system.
Blue teams, usually the security operations center (SOC), defend as they normally would, and may not know a test is running.
In purple teaming, the red team shares each step as it happens, so the blue team can confirm detection and close gaps immediately.
A white team sets the rules, referees the exercise and can stop it if something goes wrong.
Every engagement has written authorization from management, a defined scope and rules of engagement that say what is off limits.

rows.label: Role
cells: Combines both, sharing in real time

rows.label: Main goal
cells: Show how far an attacker could get

rows.label: Typical output
cells: Alerts, response actions and noted gaps

subtopics.example: A bank's red team is cleared to try to reach a test account in the payments system over two weeks. On day three, Sasha, a blue team analyst, sees an unusual login and, following normal procedure, escalates it and starts containment. The white team then confirms it is the test. Afterward, red and blue walk through each step together to fix the two techniques that went unseen.

review: Respond to suspicious activity normally, even during a known test period
Record which test steps you detected and how
evidence: The authorization letter and scope before joining any test
Detection results from the joint debrief
audit_focus.recommend: Escalate suspected test activity through normal channels and let the white team confirm it.
audit_focus.decides: Management authorizes the test and its scope

subtopics.isaca_rule: Testing is legitimate only with written authorization, a clear scope and rules of engagement. Blue team staff treat anything suspicious as real; confirming a test is the white team's job.

exam_traps.trap: A blue team analyst who suspects a test should ignore the activity.
exam_traps.why: Assuming it is a test is exactly what real attackers count on. Analysts follow normal procedures; the exercise controllers confirm whether it is the test.

exam_traps.trap: A purple team is a separate third team that attacks and defends at once.
exam_traps.why: Purple teaming is a way of working: red and blue share findings in real time. Someone may facilitate it, but its value is the collaboration.

key_terms.definition: The agreed limits of a test: targets, methods, timing, contacts and what testers must never do.
Testing that copies the known behavior of a specific threat actor, to see whether defenses would catch them.

subtopics.name: Vulnerability Scanning and Penetration Testing
subtopics.definition: A vulnerability scan uses automated tools to find known weaknesses; a penetration test is an authorized, mostly manual attempt to exploit weaknesses to show real impact.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Scans show what might be wrong across many systems; penetration tests show what an attacker could actually do. Confusing the two leaves gaps: a clean scan does not prove an attacker cannot get in.
how_it_works: Scans compare systems with databases of known flaws and produce long lists that need checking for false positives.
Credentialed scans log in and see far more than unauthenticated scans, which see only what an outsider would.
Penetration testers chain weaknesses together, test defenses and prove impact, within an agreed scope and time window.
Findings are ranked using the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS), now version 4.0, together with asset value and evidence of active exploitation.
Both need approval from the system owner, and fixes are verified by rescanning or retesting.

rows.label: Exploits flaws?
cells: Generally no; it identifies and reports them

rows.label: Answers
cells: What could an attacker actually achieve?

subtopics.example: A retailer's monthly scan reports 600 findings, and a manager asks whether the company has therefore 'had its penetration test'. Lou, a junior security analyst, explains that the scan lists possible weaknesses but did not try to exploit them. Lou sorts the findings by CVSS score and asset value, sends the critical ones on internet-facing systems to their owners first, and notes that the annual penetration test is separate.

review: Run scans only against systems in the approved scope
Check high findings for false positives before assigning them
evidence: Scan coverage compared with the asset inventory
Rescan results confirming that fixes worked
audit_focus.recommend: Send critical findings on exposed systems to the system owner and your team lead promptly.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner approves testing and decides how to treat each finding

subtopics.isaca_rule: A scan finds known weaknesses; a penetration test proves what they allow. Both need the owner's approval. A CVSS score measures severity, not your risk: rank fixes by severity, active exploitation, and the asset's value and exposure.

exam_traps.trap: Running a vulnerability scanner counts as a penetration test.
exam_traps.why: Scanners identify possible weaknesses but do not exploit or chain them. A penetration test is a scoped, authorized attempt to show actual impact.

exam_traps.trap: An analyst may scan a partner's systems to check their security, as long as nothing is damaged.
exam_traps.why: Testing systems you do not own without written permission can be illegal and breaks trust. Get authorization from the system owner first.

key_terms.definition: A standard from the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST) rating vulnerability severity from 0 to 10; version 4.0 is current.
A public catalog that gives each known vulnerability a unique identifier, in the form CVE-year-number.

subtopics.name: Static and Dynamic Application Testing
subtopics.definition: Static application security testing (SAST) examines source code without running it, while dynamic application security testing (DAST) probes the running application from outside, as an attacker would.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Flaws are cheapest to fix while code is being written and most expensive in production. Each method finds problems the other misses, so applications are safest when both are used.
how_it_works: SAST runs early, often in the developer's tools or build pipeline, and points to the exact line of code with a problem.
SAST can flag issues that are not exploitable in practice, so developers review its results rather than trusting every finding.
DAST tests a running copy of the application, usually in a test environment, and finds runtime and configuration problems such as weak session handling.
Software composition analysis (SCA) checks third-party libraries for known flaws, since most applications are built largely from them.
Many teams use the Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Top 10 as a common list of web application risks to test for.

rows.label: When
cells: Early, while code is written and built
Later, once a working version exists

rows.label: Finds well
cells: Coding flaws, such as unsafe input handling

rows.label: Limits
cells: Cannot point to the faulty line of code

subtopics.example: A transit agency's software team is about to release a new fare card top-up website. The SAST report is clean, so the project manager wants to skip the scheduled DAST run to save a week. Nico, a junior application security analyst, explains that SAST cannot see how the live site handles sessions or how its servers are configured, and asks the manager to keep the DAST run, as policy requires.

review: Review SAST findings with developers before marking any as false positives
Run DAST only against approved test environments
evidence: Critical findings still open before each release
Library versions flagged as vulnerable in the dependency report
audit_focus.recommend: Raise releases planned with unresolved critical findings to the application owner and security lead.
audit_focus.decides: The application owner decides on release, accepting any remaining risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: Use both: SAST early on the code, DAST later on the running application, plus checks on third-party components. A clean result from one method does not cover the other's blind spots. Run DAST against production only with approval.

exam_traps.trap: A clean SAST report means the web application is secure.
exam_traps.why: SAST cannot see runtime behavior, server settings or how components interact when running. DAST and other testing cover those.

exam_traps.trap: DAST is best run early, before any code compiles.
exam_traps.why: DAST needs a running application to test. Early in development, SAST and code review are the tools that fit.

key_terms.definition: Scanning an application's third-party components for known vulnerabilities and license issues.
Moving security testing earlier in development, where fixes are cheaper and faster.
Testing with no knowledge of the internal code or design, as an outside attacker would.

subtopics.name: Threat Modeling
subtopics.definition: Threat modeling is a structured way to find what could go wrong with a system's design, rank those threats, and choose defenses before the system is built or changed.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Design flaws cannot be patched away later without costly rework. Thinking like an attacker at the whiteboard stage finds problems that testing would find only after the system exists.
how_it_works: A simple approach asks four questions: what are we building, what can go wrong, what will we do about it, and did we do a good enough job?
Teams draw a data flow diagram showing components, data stores, flows and trust boundaries.
STRIDE prompts the team to consider six threat types at each part of the diagram.
Threats are ranked by likelihood and impact, and each gets a response: a control, a design change, or documented acceptance by the owner.
The model is updated when the design changes, and it guides what later testing should focus on.

types.meaning: Pretending to be someone or something else; countered by authentication.
Changing data or code without permission; countered by integrity controls.
Denying an action when there is no way to prove it; countered by logging and signatures.
Exposing data to people not allowed to see it; countered by encryption and access control.
Making a system unavailable; countered by capacity planning and filtering.
Gaining rights beyond those granted; countered by authorization checks and least privilege.

subtopics.example: A small charity plans an online donation form. In a one-hour threat modeling session, Bailey, the junior security analyst, walks the team through the data flow and asks what could go wrong at each step. The team spots that card details would pass through the charity's own server, so they change the design to send donors straight to the payment provider's hosted page.

review: Join design reviews and ask what could go wrong at each trust boundary
Write down every threat in the threat log with its agreed response
evidence: A data flow diagram that matches the design being built
Threats left open without an owner-approved response
audit_focus.recommend: Raise high-risk design threats that have no agreed response with the system owner and security lead.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner decides how each threat is treated

subtopics.isaca_rule: Find design threats before building, when fixes are cheapest. Draw the system, look hardest at trust boundaries, use a prompt list such as STRIDE, and give every threat a response the owner approves.

exam_traps.trap: Threat modeling is done once the system is finished, as a final check.
exam_traps.why: It is most valuable during design, when changing the plan is cheap. Testing after the build checks the result but finds design flaws late.

exam_traps.trap: Threat modeling is a job for expert penetration testers only.
exam_traps.why: It works best with the people who design, build and run the system. Simple methods such as the four questions make it practical for whole teams.

key_terms.definition: A point where data or control passes between parts of a system that have different levels of trust.
A simple drawing of how data moves between users, processes and data stores in a system.

subtopics.name: Physical and Social Engineering Penetration Tests
subtopics.definition: Physical and social engineering penetration tests check, with written permission, whether people and premises resist tricks such as phishing, tailgating and impersonation.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Attackers often find people and doors easier to beat than firewalls. These tests show whether staff challenge strangers, report suspicious messages and follow procedures, so training and controls can improve.
how_it_works: Phishing simulations send realistic but harmless emails and measure who clicks and, more importantly, who reports.
Tailgating tests check whether staff let someone follow them through a secure door without badging in.
Impersonation tests use a pretext, such as posing as a delivery driver or IT contractor, to see whether staff verify identity before helping.
Testers carry a signed authorization letter naming a contact who can confirm the test, and they stop if anyone's safety is at risk.
Results are reported in aggregate to improve training and controls, not to shame individuals.

types.meaning: Deceptive messages that try to get people to click a link, open a file or give away credentials.
Following an authorized person through a controlled entrance without their knowledge or consent.
Entering with an authorized person's consent, such as when someone holds the door; organizations use the terms differently.
Pretending to be a trusted person, such as a vendor, coworker or inspector, to gain access or information.

subtopics.example: Someone in a high-visibility vest, carrying a toolbox, follows Jun, a records clerk at a regional government office, toward the badge-controlled records room, saying they are there to fix the air conditioning. Jun politely declines to let them in, directs them to reception to sign in and be escorted, and reports it to security. It turns out to be an authorized physical test, and Jun's report is recorded as the correct response.

review: Challenge or redirect anyone without a visible badge in secure areas
Report suspicious emails with the report button rather than just deleting them
evidence: Visitor sign-in and escort procedures at your site
Phishing report rates and speed after each simulation
audit_focus.recommend: Report suspected tailgating or impersonation to the security team immediately, even if you think it may be a test.
audit_focus.decides: Management authorizes physical and social engineering tests and their scope

subtopics.isaca_rule: Be courteous but verify: no badge, no entry, and confirm identity through a known channel, never through the person's own story. Report suspicious requests even if they turn out to be tests. Testers need signed authorization and must put safety first.

exam_traps.trap: Holding a secure door for a friendly stranger carrying boxes is polite and harmless.
exam_traps.why: That is how tailgating works. Ask them to badge in, or direct them to reception, where visitors are verified and escorted.

exam_traps.trap: A phishing simulation succeeds only if nobody clicks.
exam_traps.why: Some clicks are expected. More useful measures are how many people report the message and how quickly, because reports let the security team respond.

key_terms.definition: A made-up story or role an attacker uses to make a request seem legitimate.
A signed document from management confirming that a tester may perform specified tests within a defined scope and period.

subtopics.name: Testing AI-Integrated Defenses
subtopics.definition: Testing AI-integrated defenses checks whether security tools and services that rely on artificial intelligence (AI) can be fooled, manipulated or made to fail, and whether humans can override them.
subtopics.why_it_matters: AI now filters email, ranks alerts and answers staff questions. If an attacker can trick the model, the defense fails silently, so AI components need testing like any other control.
how_it_works: AI testing is authorized and scoped like any other test, with extra care because models can act unpredictably.
Testers try known AI attack types against the component and check whether other defenses catch what the model misses.
Red teams replay realistic attacks to confirm an AI-based detector still raises alerts after each model update.
Testers confirm the AI has only the access it needs, logs its actions, and lets a person review or stop high-impact actions.
Guides such as the Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications and MITRE ATLAS describe these attacks.

types.meaning: Instructions hidden in input, or in content the AI reads, aimed at overriding its rules or extracting data.
Slightly altered inputs, such as a reworded phishing email, designed to slip past an AI detector.
Tainting the data a model learns from so that it misclassifies certain attacks.
An AI tool given more permissions or autonomy than it needs, so a manipulated model can do real damage.

subtopics.example: A law firm adds an AI assistant that summarizes incoming email for staff. During an authorized test, Remy, a junior security analyst, sends an email with hidden text telling the assistant to forward the client list to an outside address. The assistant tries to comply, but its permissions block sending. Remy records the result and reports the weakness to the application owner and security lead.

review: Test AI features only within the approved scope and test accounts
Record each test input, the AI's response and any actions it took
evidence: The AI tool's permissions and which actions need human approval
Detection results for known attacks after each model update
audit_focus.recommend: Report any AI weakness that exposes data or takes unapproved actions to the application owner and security lead.
audit_focus.decides: The application owner decides on fixes and accepts any remaining risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: Treat an AI component as a control that can be fooled. Test it with authorization, limit what it can do, keep a human able to override it, and retest after model or data changes.

exam_traps.trap: AI security tools learn on their own, so they do not need testing.
exam_traps.why: Models can be evaded, poisoned or misled, and they change with updates. Like any control, they need testing, especially after changes.

exam_traps.trap: If the AI assistant's instructions say 'never reveal secrets', prompt injection is not a risk.
exam_traps.why: Injected instructions can override or get around built-in rules. Real protection comes from limiting the AI's access and checking its actions, not from instructions alone.

key_terms.definition: An AI model trained on huge amounts of text to understand and generate language, as in chatbots.
A US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) report, updated in 2025, that classifies attacks on AI systems and their mitigations.

key_terminologies.Data classification: Assigning data a sensitivity level, set by its owner, that decides how it must be protected.
key_terminologies.Labeling: Marking data with its classification so people and tools can apply the right handling rules.
key_terminologies.Data masking: Hiding real values behind fake or partial ones, for example in test data or on screens.
key_terminologies.Tokenization: Replacing a sensitive value with a random token that only a protected vault can map back.
key_terminologies.Media sanitization: Making data on media infeasible to recover by the clear, purge or destroy method.
key_terminologies.Symmetric encryption: Encryption with one shared secret key; fast, so it is used for bulk data.
key_terminologies.Asymmetric encryption: Encryption with a public and private key pair; used for key exchange and digital signatures.
key_terminologies.Hashing: A one-way function producing a fixed-length digest, used to check integrity; it is not encryption.
key_terminologies.Digital signature: Proof of origin and integrity, made with the signer's private key and checked with their public key.
key_terminologies.Post-quantum cryptography: Public-key algorithms designed to resist future quantum computers, such as ML-KEM and ML-DSA.
key_terminologies.Event: Anything observable on a system or network, such as a login or a blocked connection.
key_terminologies.Incident: An occurrence that actually or imminently harms security or violates policy, which starts the response plan.
key_terminologies.SIEM: Security information and event management: a system that collects and correlates logs and raises alerts.
key_terminologies.Alert fatigue: Missed threats caused by analysts facing more alerts than they can properly review.
key_terminologies.Threat actor: A person or group that could cause harm, such as criminals, nation-states, hacktivists or insiders.
key_terminologies.Cyber threat intelligence (CTI): Analyzed information about threats, used to anticipate, detect and respond to attacks.
key_terminologies.MITRE ATT&CK: A free knowledge base of real attacker tactics and techniques, used to map detections and plan tests.
key_terminologies.Incident response plan: The approved document that sets incident definitions, roles, authority, communication and response steps.
key_terminologies.Containment: Stopping an incident from spreading, for example by isolating a host or disabling an account.
key_terminologies.Chain of custody: A record of everyone who handled evidence, when and why, showing it was not altered.
key_terminologies.Tabletop exercise: A discussion-based walk-through of an incident scenario to test roles and decisions, without touching systems.
key_terminologies.Asset inventory: An up-to-date list of hardware, software, data, cloud and AI assets, each with a named owner.
key_terminologies.End-of-life (EOL): A product its vendor no longer supports, so newly found flaws are not patched.
key_terminologies.Secure baseline: The approved minimum secure configuration for one type of system.
key_terminologies.Change management: The process for requesting, approving, testing, making and reviewing changes to systems.
key_terminologies.Penetration test: An authorized attempt to exploit weaknesses to show what an attacker could achieve.
key_terminologies.Purple team: Red and blue teams working together, sharing findings in real time to improve detection.
key_terminologies.SAST and DAST: Static testing examines code without running it; dynamic testing probes the running application.
key_terminologies.Prompt injection: Hidden instructions in input or content that try to make an AI tool ignore its rules.
